utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no real need, I think, to delay matters -- any matters of administration at this stage. I'll say a few things about administration perhaps later. The witness before you has the advantage of protection. May he take the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The piece of paper bearing the witness's name is just being prepared. It's being given to him in the form of the top of a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look, please, at this piece of paper and just confirm if it be accurate that that is your real name. Just say "Yes" if it is so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these proceedings, you'll be known by the pseudonym K-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the piece of paper bearing his name be shown to the accused and become an exhibit. Your Honour, this witness, I should say, as with the following witness, produces fairly straightforward evidence with no exhibits or, in the case of the following witness, I think only a couple of exhibits. In each case, the witness has gone through the summary in English on a line-by-line basis and, therefore, knows that the summary -- or would be in a position to say that the summary is accurate in case that becomes relevant as a tool of abbreviating evidence. K-2, first of all, I should ask him a few questions in closed session because they might otherwise reveal his identity, and with the Chamber's leave, may we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K-2, when representatives visited -- representatives of the Red Berets visited your school in April 1995, can you remember the name of any of those who attended, any of the Red Berets who attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I remember one name; that is Radoslav Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in charge of the group attending your school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently discover what his position was in the group and what his relationship was or position was in relation to Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Radoslav Krsmanovic was the commander of the unit, as deputy of Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and some other students from your school decide to join the special forces known as the Red Berets in respect of which this visit had been paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be convenient for chronological reasons if we go to paragraph 8 and come back to paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your time with that group, of which you'll tell us in due course, did you discover whether the Red Berets had existed in any form before 1995, and if so, where they were first trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: According to the what the instructors were saying, I learnt that the origins of the Red Berets date back to Knin, in the Alfa Centar in Knin where the first training started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom had they first been trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't know the exact answer to that question, but as far as I know, the training in the Alfa Centar was conducted by Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, according to what you were told, had they first been active before 1995; in what area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as what I learnt, they were active in Kosovo, which is an area next to Sarajevo, and for a while they were also active in Herzegovina in the surroundings of Mostar and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. As a result of your accepting the invitation or applying following the visit to your school, did you receive a written decision making you a member of the state security service of the Serbian MUP, and if so, when did that decision date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I received the decision that I was a member of the state security, but this occurred much later. As far as I can recollect, I joined the unit in May, and in June or July, as far as I can recollect, we were given written decisions saying that we were members of the state security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, thereafter, was there official recognition of the JATD, or units for anti-terrorist operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The units for anti-terrorist operations were legally recognised as legal units of the MUP of Serbia in November or October 1996 at the official opening of the camp at Kula when the name acquired its official name as the unit for anti-terrorist operations of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rather than take time returning to that topic, who was present at that meeting -- at that ceremony, rather? I think it's paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Commander Krsmanovic was present, Frenki Simatovic was present, Jovica Stanisic, Captain Dragan, and Milan Martic were all present. And there were also others persons whose names I don't know. Some were from the army of Yugoslavia, and others from the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you discovered generally but also at that ceremony, who was at the top of the management tree for this organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The main person, that is our commander, was Frenki Simatovic, and he came accompanied by Jovica Stanisic as the main chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout your time with this organisation, what support, if any, what approval, if any, of your activities did the group have from the government of Serbia, as you could judge it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: We had full support in the form of ammunition, uniforms, and all other necessities and also the possibility to use camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same topic, paragraph 7, was there an occasion where there was a meeting with Simatovic and others where Simatovic said something that indicated where authority was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: This happened on one occasion. The whole unit had a meeting at the camp in Lipovica, close to Belgrade. Present at the meeting was Krsmanovic, Frenki Simatovic, and Rajo Bozovic, who said that our unit must do whatever it was asked to do, that there was no possibility of us saying that we cannot do something or that we do not wish to do something and that for those reasons the doors of the president were open to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your understanding of the doors of the president were a reference to whom or was a reference to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I was able to gather, there was only one president, and it referred to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, as far as I was able to conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6. Briefly, the structure of the state security service of the Serbian MUP, was it divided into some five centres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: There were five main centres situated in Belgrade; Nis, Novi Sad, Kragujevac, Kraljevo. After that, the state security service was divided into departments, attaches, which were under the control of operative officers who held control of a certain locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's probably enough detail for the time being. The reporting chain of the group that came to be known as the Red Berets, was that a normal reporting chain or was there anything special about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: What was special about the Red Berets was, first of all, that as members of the Red Berets, we're not allowed to talk about the unit, especially not about the activities of that unit or, in fact, about its very existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And its reporting chain, did that fit within the general structure of the Serbian MUP and the state security service or did it have a separate reporting chain, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only method of reporting was directly to Krsmanovic, and Krsmanovic was accountable directly to Frenki, and then how it went on from there, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 9. You said you weren't allowed to talk about your work. Was there a document you saw on one occasion dealing with the rules and procedures of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. There was the rules of procedure of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually read it yourself on the occasion you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some of the topics it covered reflecting some of the functions your group was authorised or expected to perform? In particular, functions that might be thought to affect or interfere with ordinary civilian human rights.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: In those rules, among other provisions, there was one regarding the way in which activities had to be conducted, and in certain circumstances, it was possible to read other people's mail, secret listening in to conversations, and also trying to win over persons to work for us. That is mostly -- that is most of what I can recollect just now regarding the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having dealt thus with some of the general knowledge you acquired about your organisation, we'll return - paragraph 10 - briefly to the chronology. In May or June of 1995, did you report for training, and to which building did you go in Belgrade to report for training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: We had to report in front of the main MUP building in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were some 30 people in number. Did you go to a makeshift training camp in Pajzos in Eastern Slavonia where you were provided with uniforms, rifle, knives, and so on, that camp being in an area between Sarengrad and Bapska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that camp near to a villa that had some historical importance or significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: That villa was within the camp compound. It was the former Tito villa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that villa used when important people visited and stayed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The villa was used exclusively for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: In those days, it was -- actually, I can't remember or, rather, I never knew his surname but his first name was Zvjezdan. Together with Mr. Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was also known as Zveki, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your own instructor was named?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Among other instructors, there was Milos Dukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Known as Duka, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Included in the people who visited the villa, can you list some of the people you saw visiting there or learnt to be visiting there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I saw Rajo Bozovic. I saw Radoslav Krsmanovic. I didn't see, but I heard that another visitor was Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact there or see any visits there from representatives of the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on several occasions, but I did not know the name of the officer in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What rank was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to training and to personnel, did you discover whether those instructing you had particular types of backgrounds; in particular, any criminal elements to their backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions when we had private conversations, we heard, regarding a couple of them, that they did have a criminal background, a criminal past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, were there two trainers who seemed to have proper police training and came to teach you about particular topics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they come from? What were they teaching you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: They came from one of the Red Beret camps at Batajnica, from the airport at Batajnica, and they taught us the martial arts and combat in general, such as the liquidation, silent liquidation, and other combat skills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Silent liquidation by use of knives and things like that, is that it? Wire and breaking of necks, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Pajzos, were there already weapons for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While there, did you see further supplies of weapons and ammunition arriving? If so, in what sort of vehicle, and how was the vehicle marked to indicate its origin? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The supplies of weapons and ammunition were conducted on a regular basis, and they would always come in with a truck with M602 number plates. M always, and usually 602. That number was characteristic for the state security centre. M602 were the licence plate numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the Serbian RDB, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed at the camp between June and October 1995, I think. You saw something on one occasion of Simatovic. Can you tell us about that and the effect he had on people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see something of Simatovic coming to the camp on one occasion, I think in a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was when I heard that Simatovic had come to the camp, intending to try out some new weapons or, rather, the Desert Eagles - that was the type of weapon - and Bozovic was there in front of the heliodrom. There was a heliodrom there and they came in by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may have also seen him on other occasions, for example, in Lipovica, and indeed at Kula, as you've told us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did he and his presence have on those in this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, starting from the lowest ranks and then via Krsmanovic upwards and the other commanders, everybody was afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn briefly, please, to Arkan's unit. See if you can help us at all with that. Did you see something of the person who you understood to be second in command of Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I saw Aco Legija. He came with another few members of Arkan's Tigers to fetch ammunition. He came to our camp in Lipovica. That's what I saw. And I saw them take this out of the warehouses and load them up onto their own jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a unit called the Boka unit operating in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. It was Boca, the Boca unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the same unit you're speaking of, is it, or is it a different unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No, they weren't Arkan's Tigers. That was another unit, a different one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... unit then, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, that particular unit was not within the frameworks of Arkan's Tigers, and they came a couple of times as well to our camp in Lipovica -- I beg your pardon, to Pajzos, to pick up ammunitions and other supplies such as uniforms, et cetera. And what was characteristic for this unit was that most of their jeeps were black with white stickers on the doors and a black Skorpion. And underneath the Skorpion, it said Boca detachment, Boca unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was it, just to be quite clear, that these supplies were made available?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that applies both to Arkan's unit and to the Boca unit, does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. The difference in their arrivals was two or three days. They would come two or three days apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions overall, roughly, did you see supplies made available to either Arkan's unit or to the Boca unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Three or four times perhaps. At least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, however, one occasion when Arkan himself arrived at the camp in circumstances where he declined to identify himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I heard about that event from a guard who was on duty at the gate at the time. His nickname was Kevin. I can't remember his exact name, his proper name. But Arkan had arrived. He came up to the gate of our camp, but there were orders that without permission from our commander, nobody was to be allowed to enter through the gate. Arkan reacted very strongly to that, and the guard called up the villa and Krsmanovic ordered him to send Arkan away from the camp, from the gate, and Arkan turned his jeep around and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, did you see the deputy Legija come to the camp and obtain supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. That was when I saw Legija and several other men load up several caskets of ammunition and hand grenades, I believe, and then they left in their jeep. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 16. Was your unit deployed at some stage to a camp in the forests of Ziriste, which is near the village of Njemci, which the Chamber can find at page 23 E-2 of the atlas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. That was an improvised camp, in fact, in a forest called Ziriste, and we spent, as far as I remember, a minimum of one and a half months in that forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your purpose in being there, as subsequently discovered, was what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I was able to gather, on one occasion we went into action quite suddenly and were deployed in a village near the demarcation line. I don't remember the name of the village, and I didn't know its name, actually. I didn't know about it. And it was along the borderline with the Croatian forces. And we were deployed in the abandoned houses on this line, and our instructors had given us orders to wait for him to give us the orders to go into action. And we were deployed there from late afternoon, along those separation lines, to the early afternoon, and the instructor came by again and told us to withdraw. The next day, in the camp, they said why we were there was to help the withdrawal of some of our forces or operatives from the -- from Croatian territory, and rumours were going around that these operations officers were walking in civilian clothes through the town of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say your operatives, do you mean particularly Red Beret operatives or do you mean other operatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I can't say exactly whether they were predominantly Red Berets, but I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The camp at Ziriste, did it also house representatives of another army, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The members of the army of Republika Srpska Krajina, and there are about 60 of them in two large tents. They were put up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did some of those migrate in a sense and become instructors in your unit? Or the other way round, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Not from that particular camp but from the Poskok unit, which was active in the area of the Republika Srpska Krajina in the form of special units, they joined us. Several members of that unit became our instructors, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was some -- was there a tent at the camp containing prisoners, ordinary prisoners, prisoners for criminal offences from Serbia, and if so, what did they tell you about their being there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. Right next to our own camp there was a tent that had been erected, with prisoners. They themselves said this. They said that they were prisoners and that they were at the front because their prison sentences would be abolished or reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going through 1995 and into 1996, throughout this time, how had you been paid for your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At that time while I was in the unit, I would be given a salary in cash, without any signature or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no paperwork identifying the unit of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your unit arrived at a training camp in Lipovica, as you've already told us, and also, did you move from there to the Kula camp near Vrbas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. After spending several days in Lipovica, we moved to the Kula camp, and this camp was officially opened a few days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that official opening, that you've already spoken about, where Jovica Stanisic, the man ultimately in charge, was present; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't, when you first answered questions about this, able to approximate a date for this ceremony. I don't know if you're able to assist the Judges at all now with what year or what part of the year that ceremony occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The ceremony, as far as I'm able to recollect, was held in the month of October or perhaps November 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until that ceremony, by what name or names was your unit known colloquially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, they referred to us as the Red Berets. That's what they called us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other name by which you were known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. They would call us "Frenki's men" or "Frenkijevci" sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the ceremony, you were known as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The unit was known as the unit for anti-terrorist operations of the state security service, the JATD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Kula to return to Lipovica, and did you make a decision to leave the unit generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. I made this decision much earlier, but it wasn't possible to leave the unit because our superiors would say that, you know, it is very difficult to become a member of the unit and it is even more difficult to leave the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you finally achieve your desire to leave the unit? Can you put a date on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: This happened in the month of March, February or March, 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have got some documents which we don't wish to weary the Judges with unnecessarily, but it may be -- would you be assisted by looking at documents to ensure that you get the year and month right for these appointments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think after you left the Red Berets, you then took up or found yourself in employment as what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I was transferred to the duties of a policeman in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month did you take up that employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll perhaps go into closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the date of the ceremony, if you have any further answers to give, do, but please don't guess as to the date if you can't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I do apologise. The ceremony took place in October or November 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One -- moving on and a small point, deal with quickly. On an occasion when travelling, were you hitchhiking and were you picked up by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. someone who identified himself as a commander of the Parachute Brigade -- the 63rd Parachute Brigade of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. That was Major Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you identify yourself as a member of the group of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. I introduced myself as a former member of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Major Ostojic appear to have knowledge of and be on good terms with people in the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: During our talk, I came to the conclusion that he knew Rajo Bozovic very well, as well as Krsmanovic and Frenki. And he even said to me that if I happened to see Rajo Bozovic, to say hello to him from him, from Major Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we must go into private session once more, it won't be for very long, and I think it is, may be the last time. May we do that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K-2, from what you learnt, what was happening in the Kosovo villages in about January 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I learnt from talking to my colleagues, the cleansing of villages had begun, and when the Albanians tried to flee from Kosovo, their ID cards were taken away from them en masse. And there were also cases when money was confiscated as well from the Albanians. There were also cases when houses, other people's houses, were looted, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with the cleansing of the villages, was the account of what was happening given you by one or more than one or by several of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Those talks involved several colleagues, four or five of us. We would be sitting around and chatting about what was happening in the field, how it had happened, and so on, and from these chats I arrived at my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a pattern of activity in the villages described to you by your colleagues? How were things done to cleanse the villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Mostly this was done in the following way: The artillery would open fire on the village. After several hours of artillery fire, the infantry would come in which would search the houses house by house throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the removal of identification papers, according to what your colleagues told you, who was removing identification papers? Which body, which force was doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The policemen were doing that at the checkpoints, the control points controlling all vehicles, passenger vehicles passing by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your colleagues explain pursuant to what order or instruction they were doing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the police officers operating in Kosovo, were there others who had been members of the Special Police Units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. There were Special Police Units that were actually formed out of the regular members of the police force. Also, there were special anti-terrorist units, known as SAJ. And I also heard that Red Berets had been present at Kosovo. And I heard from my colleagues that they had a camp at the prison in Istok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just yes or no: Did you hear from anyone of alleged involvement of the Red Berets in Racak? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes or no; did you hear of the involvement of any members of the police station from Pristina being involved in the attack on Prekaz and Likosane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I heard that they were involved in the attack against Prekaz or Likosane, that is, members of the Pristina detachment of the Special Police Unit among whom there were members of my former police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with that in two parts, the Red Berets present at Racak - just yes or no - are you in a position to give any names of the Red Berets allegedly involved at Racak? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under whose command were the officers of the special force from Pristina who were involved in Prekaz or Likosane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Under the command of Zarko Brakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see members of the Red Berets in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On one occasion, I saw them in civilian clothes at the discotheque of the Grand Hotel, and on another occasion during the bombing campaign, in front of the Grand Hotel, in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they said they were there, did they say what their purpose was in being there on either of these occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On the first occasion when we met at the discotheque of the Grand Hotel, I asked them what they were doing, and one of them said -- he didn't say anything specific, but he said, "We were doing some things." And on a second occasion, when I met them in front of the Hotel Grand, they said they were there because there was a meeting being held of senior officers, and one of the officers from the Red Berets was attending and they were waiting for him and providing security for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently see arriving at the hotel senior officers, whom you can name and whose units you can identify, consistent with their going to such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: After the meeting ended, from the meeting room in the basement of the Hotel Grand, I met in the lobby General Stevanovic and also Zarko Brakovic. And there were a couple of officers from the army of Yugoslavia. I cannot remember what their ranks were, and I didn't know their names, but they were wearing the uniform of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we get the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be the witness can't help us in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you give us the date, or the approximate date by month and year, of either of these meetings, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to recollect, this occurred in the winter of 1998, or maybe the beginning of 1999. I'm really sorry; I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the bombing campaign in Kosovo, did you at some stage, and if so, tell us when, have anything to do with providing security for convoys travelling between Belgrade and Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: When I went to Pristina for my own purposes, the only way I could go there was on a convoy that was going there and also while providing escort for those convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those convoys -- what did those convoys contain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The convoys were transporting grenades and munitions to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such convoys did you witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I travelled on three convoys. Two convoys were transporting munitions and grenades, and the third consisted of ten combat vehicles known as BOV, personnel carriers, that were going to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discover or did you see where the munitions came from and what the munitions were on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On one occasion, we were transporting first from the MUP in Belgrade. We went to Cacak, to the Sloboda factory, where we loaded grenades for mortars and for hand-held rocket launchers known as Zoljas, and these were loaded within the Sloboda factory compound. And from there, we went on to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe how the Serbian media subsequently reported the NATO bombing of that factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: There was a daily news report saying that the NATO forces had bombed a factory producing washing machines and cookers and that there was absolutely no reason for bombing that factory, whereas I personally had witnessed that in that very factory we had loaded hand grenades onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a convoy that included ten BOV armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming from where and going to where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: From the surroundings of Belgrade, heading for Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the involvement of the special anti-terrorist unit in the delivery of munitions, and if so, where was that unit based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: One of the convoys or, actually, a convoy that I didn't mention consisted of two large trailer trucks, and they went to the dairy in Kosovo Polje where the SAJ or special anti-terrorist unit of the public security service was based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken of one or it may be two civilian institutions in which weapons were stored or delivered. Was there any other use, during the NATO bombing, of civilian buildings and installations by the police or other forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On one occasion, I witnessed police forces using a warehouse in the building -- I'm sorry, I'm trying to recollect. It's a sports centre in the centre of Pristina. Boro and Ramiz, it was called. And as far as I can remember, there was a food storage facility there. I was also a witness when police forces used the Panorama building or the Rilindija building in Pristina. And they also used the building known as Kosovka or Kosovarija, I'm not sure, close to the electricity board building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us already about what you learnt of what was happening in the villages. Did you hear anything of Albanians being killed in the course of 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: There were stories that I heard from my colleagues who went into the field that quite a large number of Albanians were killed, but I never heard anyone in particular state that he had killed such-and-such a person. I was never a witness to such a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of theft of money. Did you yourself see anything of theft from Albanian houses, and if so, did you see anything of where stolen property was actually stored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On one occasion, close to my former station, there was an Albanian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. house with business premises on the ground floor, and members from my station broke into what house and took out the furniture, the computer, and other appliances, and a large office table ended up in the office of my former police commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any disciplinary measure taken against your colleagues who had been involved in this or similar activity, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to Arkan's presence, if any, in Kosovo, what did you learn of that and from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: During a conversation with one of my colleagues in the station, I learnt that after most of the operations were over, Arkan, with his units, came to Pristina. But apparently on that occasion he clashed with Frenki, because Frenki told him, "You came with your units after we had finished everything in order to plunder and loot." And on that occasion, Frenki probably chased him away from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, was there a group called Munja of which you learnt something; and if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I learnt from colleagues from my station that in the environs of Pec there was a group led by a policeman who was a member of the Special Police Unit and whose nickname was Munja. His name is not known. And the unit consisted of members of the police force and civilians from the surroundings of Pec. And that is why I heard about them, because on one occasion they successfully carried out an operation together with the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, K-2. Wait there, you will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2 of your statement, you're asking for all necessary measures to be taken to protect your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say that your life was in grave danger.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still believe that your life is in grave danger in view of the fact that from the date of your statement, it's been almost two and a half years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you still believe your life is in danger two and a half years later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, that is my belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is the reason why you believe your life is in danger your statement to the investigators or the fact [redacted] [redacted] Why is your life in danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Now for both reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that line of questioning may not itself be a subtle of way of seeking to identify the witness publicly, and we must proceed with the very greatest caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So because you're involved in the [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the main reason why you're no longer living in Serbia and why you're concealing your identity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're now living in the territory of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't see why you can't answer that question. I'm just asking whether you're working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to pursue this, Mr. Milosevic, we must go into private session. Do you want to pursue it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do wish to pursue it, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, all the questions he's asked so for are asked in relation to a statement given to the investigators of the Prosecution, and I think you need to have that statement given by the witness to the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a copy. If it's not available now, we can have it after the adjournment. Is it available?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were examined this morning about the way in which the Red Berets, within the framework of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, et cetera, existed and functioned; whether you knew who was in command, how it was organised, et cetera. Do you know that what you are saying is no secret and that these were regular units - of course they're not called Red Berets - that all regular units, either of the state or the public security service, were regularly included in the formation of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Serbia? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I am not aware of that specifically and in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are saying that the Red Berets started to exist earlier on, and then in 1995, you attended a ceremony where an anti-terrorist unit was organised, and then those Red Berets were transformed into an anti-terrorist unit. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the Republika Srpska - I have now started collecting information about all these things - do you know that virtually there wasn't a town in which there weren't some Red Berets? There were some municipal Red Berets. There were the Red Berets of Krajina, the Red Berets in Republika Srpska, in the police. There were Red Berets in the army. Did you see a chief of staff in those days also wearing a red beret sometimes, and he was not a member of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're putting a series of points to the witness. He should have the chance to answer. Witness K-2 -- wait a moment. Just one at a time. The first point that's made is that there were Red Berets in every town, municipal Red Berets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I explain this question that has been put to me by Mr. Milosevic? Mr. Milosevic, it is true that many units wore red berets, but if you did not know in certain circles, public circles, when you mentioned Red Berets, especially in circles in Belgrade and in Serbia, people knew exactly what this meant. I don't know whether you were aware of that in your circle, but in the circles I moved in, when the word "Red Berets" was used, we knew who was meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a unit under that name. I am aware of the unit for anti-terrorist activities. It exists. It is part of the establishment of the security service, and it's no secret. I don't know whether they were ever called Red Berets. As to who wore red berets during the war and who is wearing red berets today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the first point. Was there -- just a moment. Where was there anything secret about the existence of the Red Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Beret unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The main and first secret was that we were not to say that the unit existed. We were advised, as members of the Red Berets, not to talk to anyone about the existence of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that in a regular army, a soldier must not provide information about his unit, even if it is a quartermaster company of a brigade, which is concerned with supplies, food, and preparing of food? Do you know that these are customary rules? And why are you making a mystery out of this, saying that you were not allowed to say that you existed and yet you existed? And what, then, were you supposed to say, "You see me but I don't exist"? Is that the explanation you're trying to give us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No, that is not the explanation. I do know that the activities of a unit, the method of work and things like that are not revealed to the public, but when you're told not to talk about the existence of that unit -- I'll give you a concrete example. One of the commanders told us, "If anyone asks you where you're working, like your family members, it's sufficient for you to say that you're working in the ministry." We weren't even supposed to say that we were working in the state security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. We're five minutes past the usual time. We can return to this afterwards. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes. Witness K-2, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it we're in open session. You have -- Mr. Milosevic, you have an hour left, up to one hour left, I should say, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a little less than the opposing party had, Mr. May, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not at all. It is most certainly not. It is rather longer than they had, but let us go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we can skip some bits here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you were employed in the Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say that your unit enjoyed the support of the government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: Do you know that the Ministry of the Interior is also a ministry within the composition of the government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where's the problem, then, if the ministry, a ministry which is a part of that government, has its own support or, rather, that the government supports its own ministry? Where's the problem there? And its structures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any problem in your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any part of the MUP that doesn't enjoy the support of the government? Is there any part of MUP that doesn't have it? Because you emphasised that this particular part had the support of the government. Is there any part of the MUP or Ministry of the Interior that does not enjoy the support of the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that it was precisely that particular unit, the anti-terrorist operations unit is an official formation and part of the MUP of Serbia? There is no mystery there, no mystification on that score.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At the time that I was a member of the unit, there were some problems - I don't want to call them rebellions - but members of the unit were not getting any written proof whatsoever that they were in fact members of the unit and that they were working within the frameworks of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come when you received a certificate saying that you were an employee of the Ministry of the Interior? That is what it says. This certificate said that you were an employee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. I received this certificate only later on, when the members required one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "later"? I see that this certificate was issued to you in June, which is when you completed your school, your regular schooling, which was also a component part of the Ministry of the Interior, which means to say the police school or academy. And then you got a job and received a certificate testifying to the job.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The certificate does have that date, but certificates were handed over to us personally considerably later. Several months later, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about bureaucratic lateness in giving you the certificate, but the certificate did say that you were an employee of the Ministry of the Interior on the date that you became an employee and got a job there once you had graduated from school, like everybody else. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as I see here that you completed your schooling and that you were a member of that unit - on the 20th of June, 1995, you became a member - how can you talk about the activities of that particular unit before the date you joined it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I think that I have already said where I get these figures from, from -- facts from, from the stories told by my instructors, the people who trained me in my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about what you heard from somebody else. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You mentioned some names, the names of some leading people, Tuka, and some others. Zvjezdan. Do you know that the people that you mentioned were members of the police force of Srpska Krajina throughout the time that it existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as we have limited time, let's take a look at this. You explained who held what function in the Ministry of the Interior, starting out with who was the leader of your own unit, commander of your own unit, and then who was the deputy head of the state security department and the head of the security department. You mentioned Simatovic and Stanisic and so on. And these are public functions and public figures, common knowledge to everyone. Is that something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, I do know that Mr. Simatovic was special advisor to the head of the department for state security, and I also know that Mr. Stanisic was head of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that's something you could have read in the papers. You say that you look -- saw the rules of service for the state security service, and then you went on to speak about what the rules contain. Mr. Nice asked you about that. And you said that it stipulated that the state security service can perform intercepts, can listen in to conversations, tapping, and so on. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that according to those rules of service which you say you have read, that permission to place -- to monitor somebody, to intercept their conversations, could only be -- an order to that effect could only be issued by the Supreme Court and signed by the president of the Supreme Court? Is that something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't know who gives permission for work of this kind to be done, but that's what I read in the rules of service. And of course, the rules of service were a state secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course the rules of service of the state security service is a state secret. So what's strange there? What is -- so what if it's secret and confidential? I assume that there is a law according to which somebody must be - how shall I put this? - listened in to and monitored and intercepted and that the state security service can only do so pursuant to an order issued by the Supreme Court. Is that something you know or aware of? At least, that's what it was like at the time; I don't know what the situation is now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Authorisation by the Supreme Court, Mr. Milosevic, is something I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I can see you don't know about it, and it seems to me you don't know about most things, about you did go on to explain how you -- 30 of you collected in front of the MUP building. You were invited to meet there, and then went up to a camp. And you say that allegedly there was a villa there, which you referred to as Tito's villa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assignment there? As far as I understand it, you weren't put up in the villa itself. You weren't accommodated there, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, my assignment was to spend time there and to attend training on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 30 of you provided security for the building. Isn't that right? You stood guard in front of the building. And if there were 30 of you in five shifts, meant six people to a shift at the gates, at the entrance. You performed the duty of guards or porters, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did you do then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: We were deployed as members of the Red Berets who were supposed to undergo training. And as far as security for the camp itself, a large portion of the ground around the camp was mined. There were vineyards and they were mined. And there were two or three -- rather, three guard posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you were doing training there, training on the ground, in the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to describe how a helicopter arrived with Franko Simatovic in it and that he tested the Desert Eagle new weapons. Do you know that the Desert Eagle is in fact a pistol? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what? He arrived there by helicopter to try out a pistol. He didn't have anywhere else to try out this particular pistol but had to come in by helicopter especially to try that out, to see how the pistol shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: That's what happened, and that's what I know, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Then you go on to speak about some sort of improvised -- but let's round off one point first. As you underwent training, did you have any combat operations that you were engaged in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At one point I did happen to mention that we launched an operation for several hours. We were ready for action but there was no actual combat on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that later, when you were at the Ziriste camp, as you said; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you yourself said, you were there from the late morning to the early afternoon, which means a few hours; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that part of your training too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was your function at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At that time, the order given was when you get the signal via the signals officer, that we should go into action against the Croatian forces, and we were explained that they were at a distance of 200 to 500 metres away from us, that we should start operating, start shooting at their positions. And we waited for the signal to be given. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you open fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No. The order to open fire never arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your function was to provide security for the transference of certain people wearing civilian clothing on the other side to collect intelligence data. That's what I understood from what you were saying. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the rumours and stories going around the camp afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So stories round the camp again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, told by the instructors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me then, please, did you in those camps of yours, in both camps while you were there - and I see that you were there in the Red Berets for about half a year, or perhaps a month longer than half a year - did you shoot any -- a single bullet in any combat operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Not in a direct combat operation, but during training, many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you were doing train -- shooting training, marksmanship and training like any other unit; right? But did you shoot at anybody? That's what I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Not me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the other members in the unit shoot at anybody? Did they have a combat operation which involved shooting at somebody at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in an operation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what do you know, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does that mean? What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking him whether that unit had engaged in any combat operation, and he said no. Then I asked him whether he shot at anybody. He said no. I asked him, did any member of the unit shoot at anybody? He said as far as he knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did this happen? When did this shooting take place, and were you present when somebody shot at somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I wasn't directly present when somebody shot directly, if you mean one man shooting at another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean shooting at people, not a target or anything else, any other things related to training sessions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I was not directly present myself, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You mentioned a ceremony in Kula to mark a review of the troops, the unit, I assume, the unit for anti-terrorist operation belonging to the state security service of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, isn't that right, the JATD?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: It was the official opening of the camp in Kula and a review of the troops of the unit, and during the speech that was delivered on the occasion, as far as I remember, one of the commanding officers said that we were members officially of the unit for anti-terrorist operations as of that day, and as of that date on that day, our salaries, we started receiving salaries in envelopes on which it said the Ministry of the Interior. Up until that date, or up until that ceremony, the money that we received, we received directly by hand, without any signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you continued to receive cash afterwards. What changed, just this envelope?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The envelope changed and the fact that we had to sign for the salary we were given, we had received. And also on the envelope until then - we never had this before - it said the coefficient, stipulated the coefficients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes, the customary data relating to salaries, how high the salaries were, what post you occupied, et cetera; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you left the unit for anti-terrorist operations in March. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At your own request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I sent in the request much earlier, but I was allowed to leave the unit only in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean much earlier when you spent only several months there in total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I sent in a request to leave the unit one or two months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this procedure for being allowed to leave took several months. You asked to be transferred to another post outside that unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I requested to leave the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, yes, you wanted to stay on working for the Ministry of the Interior but doing something else; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At that point, this wasn't important to me but I assumed that that was so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. As far as I can see from your statement, you were deployed to the post of policeman in Pristina, a junior police officer in Pristina; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: And that was not what I requested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But did anybody force you to take up this job of policeman in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, all the people that left the unit when I left considered this to be punishment for leaving the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand. I'm not following you. When you left the unit, were you able to go, for example, and take up a civilian job or did you have to stay and work for the police force? Did anybody force you to work in the police force? Is there any policeman working in the police force because he's forced to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you forcibly work in the police force? Were you forced to work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, appropriate --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Mr. Milosevic. These are possibly identifying questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying that in the winter of 1998, when you were on sick leave, I assume you were treated somewhere in a hospital outside of Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, most of the time, as you said, you spent in hospital. On what basis then, when you were not even in Kosovo, are you giving statements about things that you heard while you were virtually out of work because of sick leave or suspension and on the basis of what you had heard from some of your colleagues in the security of the MUP building? That's what you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The colleagues that I heard what I said from were colleagues who were in the field. They were not colleagues providing security of the MUP building. And whenever I heard these stories, I was in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not working. You were not in the service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, but I had to report down there in order for the proceedings to be completed and to pick up my personal income, my salary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went there to get your salary and to report there because of the proceedings that were ongoing against you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on those occasions when you went to pick up your salary or because of these administrative reasons, you heard from various colleagues these things, and you're now testifying about things that you really know nothing about. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't know what things exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for instance, you mentioned that somebody from the state security was in Racak. Now, give me a single name from somebody from the state security who was in Racak. If you're claiming that someone was in Racak, then surely you must know at least one name of a person who was in Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I perhaps could answer this question in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you're telling us that in the winter of 1998, you met in Hotel Grand certain senior officers of the army of Yugoslavia and of the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what? So what if they were at the Hotel Grand? Certain officials of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs and the army of Yugoslavia, so what if they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand either what this means. "I saw in the Hotel Grand a general from the army or a general from the police." Are they not allowed to go to the Hotel Grand? Is this linked to any kind of crime or what does this -- what is this supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't understand this question. I think the question relates more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a comment. All the witness can say, Mr. Milosevic, is that he saw these people in Pristina at the times he said. Whether there's any significance in it is a matter for the Court to say. It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with your allegation that you were transporting some equipment in a convoy from the Sloboda factory, Mr. Nice asked you how did the television of Serbia represent the bombing of that Sloboda factory by NATO? Did it represent it as being the bombing of a factory for household appliances, washing machines, cookers, and so on, and you explained that yes, our propaganda represented it as being bombing of a civilian facility. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No, that's not right. That was the conclusion that I myself made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. It was your own conclusion. And do you really know that the household appliances factory was destroyed, where hundreds of people worked, called Sloboda of Cacak? The whole of Cacak knows that, that Sloboda was destroyed, a factory manufacturing refrigerators, cookers, et cetera, and other household appliances. It was a factory of household appliances. It had an entirely civilian programme. Do you know that that factory really was bombed and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what has that destruction, that wild and savage bombing of a household appliances factory where people were employed, citizens of Cacak made their livelihood for their families, what has that got to do with any kind of munition that you were transporting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to conclude, first of all, NATO statements were that they were targeting military facilities and facilities linked to the production of weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you concluded that this factory manufacturing household appliances was also involved in the production of weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But that factory was indeed destroyed. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't any propaganda on the part of Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to understand, what was involved was that the factory was represented such as it was, that is, a factory manufacturing household appliances, but also, as far as I know, within the framework of that factory hand grenades were manufactured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Sloboda is not just one plant. The plant for household appliances was destroyed. Surely you cannot mean that such a factory can produce weapons. Sloboda is a large company, consisting of several factories or plants. Are you claiming that beneath the household appliances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness has said is that they went there and they loaded up grenades. That's what he said he got from the factory. That's his point. Now, you can call other evidence, if you want to, about this factory. It may be that it was doing both things at the same time, but we'll have to see. The witness can only say what he saw and heard himself. Is there anything, Witness K-2, that you want to add to what you said about this factory? You've heard the point that the accused makes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing more in addition to what I have said. I don't know any more details about that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you were on sick leave at the time, and you used the convoys going there simply as a means of transportation, you were not on active duty in that connection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I was not, but as I was told by a certain officer from the MUP, if the need should arise, I could provide security and I should provide security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know what they were transporting? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, in wooden, green boxes nothing else can be transported but munitions and grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw these green wooden boxes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, on which there was an inscription saying "hand grenades."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that various civilian facilities were used in Pristina, like warehouses, the department store of Kosovo, and other warehouses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
