utterances.text: So what? Why -- what's wrong if the warehouses were used? Was somebody using warehouses illegally for some reason? Do you find some irregularity in that again? What's wrong with using warehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not understand again whether this question is addressed to me or to the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You used the expression "There were stories"; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, what you're saying you're saying on the basis of stories.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Certain things, yes. I think I said which things I'm talking about on the basis of stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you participate in when you were in Kosovo? We've already established that you didn't fire a single shot when you were in training. When you were in Kosovo, did you take part in any combat operation, a single combat operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why, then, are you using in your statement the expression "the massacre in Racak"? How do you know there was a massacre in Racak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Racak, and you were not there, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you mentioned and used the term "the massacre in Racak." Do you know that in Racak the police clashed with the very strong terrorist group of Albanian terrorists or, if you like, the KLA, as they called their organisation, and there was a conflict between the two sides in which a certain number of people were killed? So why are you talking about the massacre in Racak? Is this your expression or an expression used by those who were investigating you, interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe there was a massacre in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Definitively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did you hear was happening in Racak, since you're being asked about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that in Racak, the killing was carried out of several -- I can't claim now whether they were civilians or members of the KLA, but as far as I know, there was a mass killing and those bodies were found in a ditch somewhere. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know anything about Racak. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only significance of his evidence is what he says he heard about it from colleagues of his. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since, as you say, you abandoned the unit of your own free will and were assigned to work in Pristina as of March 1996, did you abandon the unit because you found the training too exhausting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the 1st of March, you were assigned to the position of junior policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the lowest possible level in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: It is the level at which you start working upon completing secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's the lowest level in the police; is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you were assigned to this post of a beginner with the lowest rank, what job were you given to do? As I see from the decision given to you, it was some kind of security, like a porter, a receptionist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No. I was given a job as a member of a patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you worked like a patrolman in the street, and you patrolled certain streets or a certain block of buildings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as a beginner policeman with the lowest rank, do you consider yourself to be qualified to assess the structure of the police, the public security, the state security, the activities of the police force in Kosovo, et cetera, et cetera, and all these other things that you have spoken about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: These were the things I was taught about during my schooling in the school of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I don't think that they're any assessments of my own. These were the things we were taught about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you learnt in this school of Internal Affairs. That's what you've been testifying about here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, when speaking about the structure of the state security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And as working -- while working as a policeman in Pristina, did you ever receive from your superiors any kind of order against citizens, members of the Albanian ethnicity, or that you should do anything that would be discriminatory in nature? Did you ever receive from any one of your superiors any such order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that before the accident you were suspended but not in connection with what I just -- I read out to you from the documents given by the other side to me, but - this is on page 15, the second paragraph of your statement - because of complaints in connection with the registration of a vehicle. Were you suspended because of those complaints or because it was established that you had taken part in certain illegal operations in connection with the registration of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No unlawful activities were mentioned in connection with that event, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say on page 15 that you were suspended because of complaints in connection with the registration of a vehicle. That's what you've said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: It is. It's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If something was legal, why were you suspended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Because when I was to register that vehicle owned by a person from Pristina, I could use that possibility because I came from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I couldn't complete the task. And then the person came to my commander to complain why I hadn't completed this. However, when I came back to Pristina, I explained what had happened. I returned his documents to him, and everything else. However, the commander suspended me because this was considered to be unlawful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's not dwell on that any more. So you wanted to abuse the fact that you were coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina to assist that person to illegally register his vehicle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: That's the way you're putting it, but that's not how I consider it to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But as you say on page 15, in the second paragraph, after this accident that you had later on, you couldn't work on the ground and so you were assigned to the police station in charge of providing security of the main MUP building in Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, as you were never in the field from the moment you were suspended and after that you provided security, on what basis are you testifying here about some sort of cleansing, then you're asked about the pattern of behaviour, you said first there was shelling and then the infantry and so on. On what basis are you talking about these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: On the basis of conversations with my colleagues who did go into the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names, the names of those colleagues who told you that first a village would be shelled, et cetera? There was a person who took part in this and explained that the expression "cleaning up" meant action against terrorists and not cleansing of civilians. A participant testified to that effect. And you said that you heard from your colleagues that Albanians were being cleansed. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, I never stated that the word "cleansing" or "cleaning" meant cleansing of the entire Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the terrorists, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I didn't say that it applied to terrorists only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did it apply to if it was not to civilian population and not to terrorists? Who did it apply to; to beetles and flies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: This operation which is known as cleansing or cleaning, if no one is left in the village and all the houses are burned down, then I'll be so free as to ask you, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see, according to the question by Mr. Nice, that first there was an artillery attack, then infantry goes in, and then house-to-house searches? Where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I said that I hadn't seen that. I heard that from talks to colleagues who went into the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're testifying about what you heard or allegedly heard, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I say in my statement that I heard about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You say that in October 1998 you also saw some members of the Red Berets, five or six of them, in fact, and that you knew nobody, none of them, and that there was an officer amongst them, a Red Beret officer, but you don't know which one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I said that I saw a group of Red Beret members and that I knew one of them, and I talked to one of them, and they said that they were there to provide security for the meeting and that they were waiting for a Red Beret officer to turn up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what then? What's the point? They were there to provide security for a meeting, some kind of meeting. Where was the meeting? What meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: In the conference hall of the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, the conference hall of the Grand Hotel. And who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I've already said that to the best of my recollections I saw General Stevanovic, Zarko Brakovic, and I also saw two or three - I can't remember exactly whether there were two or three - officers of the army of Yugoslavia there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what you're saying is very high-ranking officials of the police force and army that were holding a meeting in the conference hall; right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time there was terrorism in Kosovo, was there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is there something abnormal about the fact that high-ranking officers of the army and police were there for a meeting, that somebody provided security to prevent them from being shot down dead or from a terrorist diversion because the meeting was being held in a hotel, a public place where there was a lot of coming and going? Is that something out of the ordinary then, according to you, that they would have security details to ensure their security. And if the generals of the police force and army were there, that they should have security details, somebody to see that they were protected while they were in conference and not be killed by the terrorists that were rampant in Kosovo at the time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing strange about that, but the reason for which I said that I had met members of the Red Berets was to say that their presence was there at that time, that they were in Kosovo at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what if they were in Kosovo? It's no secret that the anti-terrorist unit was there. Do you know that if there was terrorism in Kosovo, isn't it logical that an anti-terrorist unit would be there, or at least part of an anti-terrorist unit would be in place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I have more to ask you. You're talking about Kosovo, and in addition to Racak, and I asked you about that and can see that you know nothing about it, you meant Prekaz, Likosane, Kacanik, were you personally in any one of these places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I mentioned these particular places because my colleagues or friends were there, and they were engaged in operations in those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you heard once again from them that where they were there was fighting, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that's what I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you that they had committed any crimes over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what were they doing there? They were fighting terrorists. They clashed with the terrorists. Do you know, for example, that those were all places where terrorist groups were very strong? So they risked their lives to defend the country from terrorism. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us on that point? It seems a very general one. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, next question. You've got about three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only three minutes, I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember this: As you were -- or, rather, how many Serbs, your colleagues, policemen, soldiers, and civilians were killed in Kosovo by the terrorists during the time that you were on sick leave? Did you talk about that, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about it, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I also know that many of my colleagues lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who do you think killed them, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The terrorists did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, in a single sentence you say that you heard about the killing of Albanians but that you did not see anything. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about the fact that your fellow colleagues were killed by terrorism, you say nothing about that, and you're a policeman yourself. And your friends were killed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, then, please, did you testify -- did you see all the destruction of the NATO bombings, because you were in Pristina all the time and then you would come and go from time to time. Do you know of all the destruction that the NATO bombing caused in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know what you have in mind exactly, but I was a witness to the fact that many buildings were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many buildings destroyed, you say. Do you know how many civilians were killed and fell casualty there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember a single policeman, a colleague of yours, who was killed without any reason in Kosovo? Can you quote me any example of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't remember anybody being killed, but I know that they were -- some people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: In BH territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any more questions on that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Do you remember where you were on the 20th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript should reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a few questions, but I should like to ask my first questions in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to start off by asking you, Mr. Witness, Witness K-2, something about what you said in your statement, the statement you gave to the investigators. And in that statement you mentioned the Green Berets, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean by the "Green Berets." What does the term imply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about May 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. The Green Berets, to me, meant, as far as I knew, a military formation, a military unit, which was composed exclusively of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a military or paramilitary unit at that time, May 1992, that is to say before there was recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I really didn't know at the time how the unit was defined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the country existed, which was in existence at the time, that is to say Yugoslavia, and Bosnia was a part of that Yugoslavia, those military units which were armed, the Green Berets, were they something that belonged to the -- did not belong to the army of Yugoslavia but paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: From what you've just said, it would appear that that's so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, not according to what I said, but that was how it was. And if that's your answer, if you say yes, then let's move on. On page 3, paragraph 2 of the English version of your statement you said that a close relative of yours had to flee from Tuzla because the military garrison in Tuzla was surrounded by those same Green Berets. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your witness statement - and may the statement be shown to the witness - it is on page 3 of the B/C/S, second paragraph, and that's what you talk about. You say that the Green Berets were -- had surrounded the garrison and that they had to flee across Mount Vlasic because of the activities of the Green Berets. Would you have a look at that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Would you help me with the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is paragraph 2, sentence 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the military garrison was surrounded by the Green Berets and that the soldiers in the garrison were endangered and that they had to take cover and defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. According to what my relative said, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Asked by the Prosecutor, you spoke about the training you underwent when you became a member of the special unit and, inter alia, you said that you did training in what you called silent liquidations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever put into practice what you were trained to do anywhere? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Except in training, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the events in Croatia in 1991 and 1992? The fighting between certain military units. Do you yourself know anything specific in view of the period of time in 1991 and 1992 you were there? In view of your age, actually..

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No. Specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events except for what you say you saw referring to the Green Berets in Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1994? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I know what everybody else knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you yourself took part in anything linked to the activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina up until 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 13 of the B/C/S version, and in the English it's page 12, the last paragraph of page 12, you even state that not even in 1995 during the Storm operation, you never received instructions to intervene. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I remember, during the Storm operations and that particular period of time, I myself was in the Ziriste camp, and all we knew about it was that one night we heard, via the communications devices, that Krajina had fallen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you had no part in any of that, nor did anybody caution you or ask you to go into action even at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I just remembered that at that particular time, our unit, the one that was in Ziriste, was on a state of alert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether what you say in your statement is true, that, "during Operation Storm we never received instructions to intervene." Is that correct? Is what you say in your statement correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a few other questions with respect to what went on in Kosovo. You were in Kosovo. You were in the area from 1996 onwards with the slight interruption while you were on sick leave. It was rather a lengthy sick leave. And you also say in your statement -- you talk about Racak in your statement, Prekaz and Likosane too. Now, do you happen to know in all three cases, in Racak, you talked about Racak, but let's take Prekaz and Likosane, that there was a conflict there between the KLA members and the regular units of the police and army of Serbia? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the presence of the KLA in the territory of Kosovo? That is, the numerical strength of the KLA and about the conflict that existed between the KLA and the regular forces of the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I knew that members of the KLA were present in Kosovo, but as for their number and other things that you asked me about, I was not familiar with. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that first conflicts would occur between the army and the police on the one side and then the KLA and that this necessarily involved casualties on both sides and among civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is really advancing a case which is, I think, a matter of judgement by the Tribunal in due course, and presenting as decided fact, almost, matters which will be controversial in due course. I'm very doubtful -- I beg your pardon: I invite the Chamber to be concerned about the value of this form of cross-examination from somebody's whose role is as an amicus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the point being, Mr. Tapuskovic, that you should be putting -- the Prosecution is saying what is relevant, what will help the Tribunal, rather than putting forward a case on behalf of the Serbs or anybody else, particularly about these matters about which there's a great deal of evidence anyway about what happened in Racak, and we're going to have to make our minds up. Perhaps you could move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't dwelling on Racak. I was referring to the awareness of this witness about certain events, though this was covered in the examination-in-chief, but he didn't mention to what extent the KLA was present in this area, how many men were under arms. I'm not asking him about anything else. Surely it is not possible for the witness not to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know - that's all I'm asking of you, Witness K-2 - except for you to tell me what you may know, if you spent so much time there, about the presence of the KLA and conflicts between the KLA and regular police and military forces. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I have direct knowledge that the conflicts started much later. Conflicts between the KLA and the police and army of Yugoslavia were preceded by terrorist attacks on police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there casualties among the policemen and the civilian population of both ethnicities? To me, I make no distinction between Albanian and civilian casualties, but I'm just asking whether there were casualties on both sides - and I'm talking about civilians - because of the conflicts between the KLA and the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I was never an eyewitness of civilian casualties, but I did eyewitness the wounding of one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the population was on the move, both Serbian and Albanian, seeking shelter, away from the places of conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we really are getting too far from the witness's evidence. We have much other evidence about these matters which we will have to make our minds up about. Now, this witness -- what this witness may have heard in particular about that is not going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't referring to what he heard but what he witnessed. As he was a witness of the bombing too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to what extent Kosovo was bombed and whether it was the area that was most bombed within the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you too in danger? Were there bombs falling close by? Were you an eyewitness of the bombs falling on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether the police obtained any information that the bombs falling on Kosovo contained depleted uranium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me also, when the bombing started, was it only then when the population started fleeing Kosovo, the Albanian population in the first place but also Serbians as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as I know, the fleeing of the population started then. Yes, you're right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: You commented on the way the media in Serbia represented the events in connection with the Sloboda factory. And did the world media show what had happened in Racak, Likosane and Prekaz, and did they represent it only as the killing of civilians, a massacre in Racak, as it was described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We dealt with one particular --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We dealt with one particular matter which he had knowledge of, which is this factory, the Sloboda factory. Now, this is a general point about which there is much other evidence, and we won't be assisted by this witness telling us what he knew about the media, particularly the world media. We shall be the judges of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not in Cacak. He wasn't there where the factory was, but he was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please. Let us move on. Now, have you got any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was my last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're past the break time, but we haven't had an hour and a half yet. Are you going to be very long with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got half a dozen questions or so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About half a dozen questions or so. I will probably be five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with them, if you can, in the five minutes available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the adjournment, if you could locate the document which the accused referred to which is related to the higher -- some committee's decision, appellate decision about the disciplinary action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have that document, and -- I gather that it's in fact attached to the witness statement you have. It hasn't been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got a lot of exhibits. We can deal with them very briefly. The only ones -- I have not found it amongst these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, there been a recent translation. I'll deal with that over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K-2, first, you've been asked several questions about your motivation for giving evidence. You said partly connected with problems or concerns you have, but what was your motive for giving evidence? Just tell the Judges. If this is going to reveal your identity in any way, we'll ask for closed session, but otherwise, tell us publicly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I think I could explain that more clearly in a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked by the accused questions suggesting that the unit in which you were engaged was a regular unit in all respects. Can I ask you a few questions arising from that? To your knowledge, did this unit engage in straightforward intelligence work of any kind or on any occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The work that the unit did, as far as I know, to my knowledge, was exclusively of a combat nature, combat type of action, which meant going out into the field and combat action exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you spoke on two occasions of these people being in civilian clothes, one at the meeting that I'll come to in a minute in Pristina, I think, but another when you were engaged in assisting the recovery of members of the Red Berets from across the border. Was it your experience that they operated in plainclothes -- in civilian clothes from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: As far as assistance of my unit to pulling out operatives from Croatian territory, there were talks in the camp that the members -- now, I can't say -- I'm not quite sure whether they were members of the Red Berets or whether they were operatives from the state security service, but at any rate, I know that there was talk of, and I'll try and quote once again, that, "Our people last night and yesterday walked around Osijek in civilian clothing." That's what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding of the reason for this regular force operating in that way in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have an objection to make. The witness is not saying that they were members of the Red Berets who were wearing those civilian clothes, and he even emphasises that he does not know that they were members of the Red Berets wearing civilian clothes at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us clarify with the witness what he meant. I certainly understood that, but I may have been wrong. Mr. Nice, perhaps you would clarify that matter, the accused having objected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The people said to have been operating in Osijek, were they Red Beret members or not or wasn't it clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I can't say with certitude. I can't say 100 per cent that they were members of the Red Berets. But as I have already stated, in the camp, among us, among members of my unit, there was talk, and once again I quote, that, "Our people last night were --" and I assume our members, that's my conclusion, that the members of the unit walked around Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even if they weren't members of the Red Berets, they were members of which service coming from which country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: The only conclusion I can make was that they were members of the state security service, 100 per cent they were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the year of this operation, if you can help us, just to be quite clear, or the date, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't remember the exact date. As far as I'm able to recall, it was sometime in the autumn of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, on the scope of operations of the Red Berets, was anything -- in light of the questions asked of you, was anything said to you or did you learn anything about the Red Berets operating overseas? Or not overseas; outside Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: Let me go back to the meeting in Lipovica, the meeting we had with Mr. Frenki and Rajo Bozovic and Mr. Krsmanovic. We were told that our unit existed -- and it was not important for purposes of action whether it was on Yugoslav territory or outside Yugoslav territory. Our unit could go into action and must indeed go into action where the need arises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the meeting of senior military and/or MUP officials in Pristina, was there anything known to you to suggest that the Red Berets' presence there was simply limited to the role of protection of those attending the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: At that particular moment, and the members of the Red Berets were exclusively in front of the entrance to the Grand Hotel and in the hotel hallway, and that was the place I met them and where I had the talk that I spoke about earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: They were dressed in NATO pattern uniforms, and they were much better equipped than the other regular units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question relates again to Zveki or Zvjezdan. It's suggested that he was a member of the police force of Srpska Krajina. Did he ever indicate that to you or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-2
utterances.text: No. I heard about this from Mr. Milosevic for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Oh, yes, there is one other matter I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm afraid this will have to be in closed session, but it's a very short point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K-2, that concludes your evidence to the Tribunal. Thank you for coming to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the Chamber is necessarily in, to some degree, confidential session or private session as the witness withdraws, can I use that time very briefly to make -- deal with a couple of things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of them has to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while again we're in -- we're in open session and Your Honour knows some of the procedural possibilities that I'm canvassing and the documents I've served on the Chamber and, of course, the consequence of those possibilities in terms of real time, something that we probably should have in mind, as a matter of interest while we're waiting for the next witness to come in, I took an hour and ten minutes in chief with the last witness. My calculation, by experiment, is that the summaries can be read at roughly the rate of -- by whomsoever they're read, take about three minutes per page, so that the various possibilities for such a witness would be if anyone were to read his statement aloud in full, to save something in the region of 40 minutes or more for a witness and to save considerably more time, of course, if the summary of the statement is taken as the evidence in chief. I realise these are matters for later consideration but it's probably helpful to have the practical realities in mind as we look at this type of witness. The next witness, then is Robert Hausvicka, and his summary is only, I think, six pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind going on until 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be referring to pages of the atlas, for your convenience, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. In what sense is this abbreviation being made? This witness was not announced as a witness until last night. He wasn't even on any kind of list. So I assume that we need to hear his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a suggestion they're making. It's a proposal that they're making, which we're going to discuss in due course, but no change for the moment. The evidence will be given in the normal way. And you won't have to cross-examine this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This witness is listed on a schedule on the 18th of December. His particular position may have accelerated for reasons outside our control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dubrovnik is shown in our Exhibit 336 on page 37.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: My name is Robert Hausvicka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hausvicka, did you live in Mokosica, some ten kilometres from Dubrovnik? We can see it on the map. Did you complete compulsory military service in Sombor in Serbia in December of 1990? Are you currently vice-president of the Dubrovnik branch of the Croatian Association of Camp Detainees of Serbian and Montenegrin Concentration Camps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the ZNG in May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a newspaper advertisement and joining a unit that was incompletely defined and simply then called the Dubrovnik Unit, counting about 100 men at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that early stage, did you all have weapons and uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there some sharing of weapons because of the insufficient number of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in August of 1991, did you join the Croatian special police force, along with friends who also had military or police training, special forces then numbering about 50?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of those, were they local to the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based, I think you say -- well, just tell us where it was based, because I don't think we can see it on the map. Yes we can. Plat, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just north-east of Mokosica, with which the Chamber is familiar. Can we turn to the attack on the Dubrovnik region. On what day and indeed at what time did that attack begin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The attack started on the 1st of October, at 6.25 a.m., in the area of Rijeka Dubrovacka, or to be more precise, Komolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The attack was in what form, coming from where?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The attack was in the form of shelling of the water supply system, the electricity power lines and telephone exchange, and it came from the direction of Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is on the Bosnia-Herzegovina border?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the phone lines as well at that time and the main road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The phone lines were immediately cut off after the first shelling, and the main road was also shelled so that there was no communication between Dubrovnik and Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any Croatian police or military presence in Mokosica at that time? If not, where were there Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: There were no army or police forces in Mokosica, but as far as I know, at frontier places there were such forces at Debeli Brijeg and two other localities; Osojnik and Brgat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mokosica shelled starting on the 1st of October and for several days? If so, how many days, and can you please tell us how many shells?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The shelling started on the 1st of October in the evening and continued for the next few days. On the 2nd of October was intensive shelling of the area of old Mokosica when the civilian buildings and local church were hit. I counted about 850 shells, but there were in fact more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your function have been to defend where you were living and the town of Dubrovnik had you been able to do so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. My mistake. Were you there to defend the town, if you could, in the force in which you were engaged?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The function of my unit was in the event of hostile attacks, that is of any attacks, to defend the city, but I wasn't able to do so because I happened to be in Stara Mokosica in my native home at the time of the shelling, the house I was born in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all you were doing, I think, was in a shelter, listening to the shells; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Mokosica, were there several shelters in which civilians could take refuge; those civilians coming from the town but also surrounding towns, villages, and parts of the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: In the area of the new settlement or New Mokosica, there were five or six nuclear shelters where civilians could seek shelter, and they did come from the surrounding places and sought shelter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there one particular shelter in a suburb where civilians were killed? And we'll turn to those deaths in a minute, but was there such a shelter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of New Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that shelter also home to the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff being the body organising support for communities in times of emergency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you near to the shelter at the time when the civilians were killed, and if so, will you tell us, please, how those deaths occurred.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: I was quite close, some 100 to 150 metres away from the shelter. The entrance to the shelter was such that people came out of the shelter to smoke because they couldn't smoke inside. And when the shell fell, there were seven civilians outside who were killed who happened to be there by chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to the names of those who were killed, there was a police car that had parked there for some reason; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: There was a police vehicle, but that car was there from the beginning of the shelling. Somebody, I don't know who exactly, came home in that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this shelling occurred on which of the days of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: When the civilians were killed, I think it was on the 7th of October that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this police car had been in the same position, for anybody to see, for several days or for six or seven days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The car was there. Was there anything in the nature of a flow of civilians into and out of the shelter that might have been visible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. The civilians would frequently come and go from the shelters because they couldn't collect all the things from their apartment, and they would go back to their apartments when there was a pause in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of, could you see the position from which the shelling by the JNA was coming?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: You couldn't see exactly from the new settlement of Mokosica, but we knew that it came from Ivanica and the surrounding hills because the army had already taken control of those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge of your home locality, what view of Mokosica would the JNA have had from their vantage point in the hills?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: It's a high ground above the new settlement and Old Mokosica, and they could see clearly, and with binoculars they could observe everything that was going on down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people were there in each of the shelters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Roughly 300 to 400 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that people left the shelters to go to their homes in quiet times, did everybody leave or were there some who were cautious, who stayed behind so that there would be less than the total numbers seen flowing in and out, or did all 300 or 400 people go in and out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Well, of course not. There were those who were more courageous than others. The braver ones would go back to fetch their belongings. But there was a place in front of the shelter, a tap of water, and all the persons in the shelter had to go out to get water from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What percentage of the people in this shelter, as indeed perhaps in the others, but in this shelter, what percentage of the people in this shelter were, like you, members of a force?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: There were five of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five out of 300 or 400?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were killed outside your shelter killed by one shell or more than one shell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: More than one shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many altogether? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Those men who were killed in front of the shelter, those seven, were killed by one shell, and another two were killed by a second shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask the witness now, please, to look at part of what is already Exhibit 361, tab 35. It's been annexed to your summary this morning for ease of reference. We can lay it on the overhead projector and the witness can help us, I think, with certain names. The document, for those seeing it, viewing it from outside, is page 63 of the indictment, and it lists various locations and various alleged deaths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look, please, Mr. Hausvicka, at this document. Beside the 7th of October and Mokosica, there are a total of nine names. Are you able to help us with which ones of those names relate to people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed in this shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? Do I need to read out the names or just show you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whichever is convenient, but we see a block of nine names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be perhaps permitted to lead on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go through these names, are you in a position to identify as having been killed seven of the names, you not being, I think, in a position to deal with Jozo Brajovic and Ivo Maskaric.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The others you know yourself, saw yourself - whatever - were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 -- paragraph 7. I think the bodies were kept in the shelter and transferred the following day by boat to Gruz.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear subsequently on the radio of a cease-fire that had been negotiated between the JNA and Croatian representatives and learn that it was said to be safe now to return to your village as others could return to theirs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. The news was broadcast on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that, and the Chamber can see the geographical point in the atlas, I think - I've just lost it again - just above Dubrovnik and just slightly to the north-west of Mokosica. Notwithstanding that, was there an advance by the JNA on the 18th of October, and if so, where to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The radio broadcast the news that people could return to the village of Osojnik because a cease-fire had been negotiated, but the JNA continued its attack and entered the village of Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it was between the 13th of October and the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, with other special police officers and regular policemen and some armed civilians, attempt to form a defensive line? If so, where?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: We tried. On the 18th of October, 1991, in the village of Pobrezje, which is just below the village of Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is not shown on the map, it being too small. With what success did you do this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: My opinion was that it was unsuccessful because JNA units that were stationed above us could see every move we made, and we could see their mortar batteries as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened to the occupants and indeed the houses of Pobrezje?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The village of Pobrezje, the people had sought shelter, and among the houses, many were damaged. There were three or four holes in each of the houses from projectiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and your fellow defenders take occupation of the houses at some stage or take up positions within those houses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. We took up positions within those houses, that is, those that we thought were a little safer than others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, from within the houses or on the way there, able to see the batteries of mortars lined up above you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: On a hill above the village, one could see a mortar battery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on from these particular events towards the end of October or the beginning of November - I think there may be an error on your -- at paragraph 10 - how much of the town of Dubrovnik had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now have, please, Exhibit 336, at page 37. If it could be placed on the overhead projector so the witness, who hasn't been in the court before -- if you could place that on the overhead projector for the witness. No, it's in front of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you would be good enough to look at the overhead projector and with a pointer point out the various places that we're going to referred to. Point it out on the projector, not on the television screen.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Could I hear the question once again? I don't quite understand what I need to show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't had a question yet. That's my mistake. By the beginning of November, to what extent had the JNA forces advanced on Dubrovnik? Can you point out the relevant towns or villages to which they had advanced? And tell us, as you're going through them, what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: The Cilipi airport, Orasac, Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as to Mokosica itself, is that, which we can see well shown on the map to the north of Dubrovnik itself, was that reached by the JNA or was that still in possession of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: That was still free. At that time, they hadn't reached Mokosica yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the other direction, coming up from Montenegro, do you know or can you help us with how far they had advanced by the beginning of November? You've spoken of the airport at Cilipi. Is that the level of their advance or the extent of their advance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: I can't know exactly because I wasn't in that area. I think they came to somewhere between Cavtat and the Cilipi airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of October of 1991, did you leave the village of Pobrezje to report to your superior, a man called Kreso Mandic, by telephone, and to do that you had to go to Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were unable to make the call, and on your return to Pobrezje, did you discover that it was under heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in the new settlement of Mokosica, a stronger attack began, using all sorts of weapons on that village, the village of Pobrezje, and my friends had withdrawn, and I moved on upwards to see what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then seek to return once more to Mokosica, but were you intercepted by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: From the Novi Nazlije, a new settlement of Mokosica, I started out towards Pobrezje to see what had happened to my colleagues. When I arrived in the village of Pobrezje, I saw a group of some 20 soldiers. I thought they were my friends, but when I came to within 20 metres of them, I realised they were JNA forces, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: I was wearing a camouflage uniform with police insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: When I realised that these were JNA forces, I did an about-turm in my car, but I assume they realised that a car was coming up towards them, they intercepted me, and started shooting at the car. At that point I thought should I kill myself or not. I had a hand grenade hitched up in my belt, but when I got out of the car I put my -- or should I get out of the car and put my arms up and surrender?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event, what happened to you? What did the JNA soldiers do to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: They came up to me very cautiously and told me to lie down beside the car, which I did, and then when they came up to me, they started hitting me, kicking me, hitting me with their rifle butts and goodness knows what else. And then one of the members, I suppose he's a member of the JNA, with a long beard, he placed a knife at my throat, and I suppose he wanted to slit my throat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he deterred from doing that by another JNA officer who instructed that you be taken to the command post for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you indeed taken off to Osojnik to be interrogated? If so, what happened on the way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did take me off to the command post at Osojnik. On the way there, as we went down the road, with all the beating that I received, I saw in passing that there were several mortars. And as the road descended towards the village of Osojnik, there were two recoilless guns, cannons, and you could see from that position Gruz, and Lapad and Dubrovacka Rijeka; you didn't have to have binoculars to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the soldiers do to you on the way to Osojnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: While we were walking towards the elevation, they kept beating me and whatever, and then they threw me into a military vehicle and took me to a tent. In the car or military vehicle, military off-road vehicle, they also beat me. And at one particular point, one of the three men who were with me cut my ear. He wanted to cut my ear off, in fact, because I had an earring in my left earlobe, and he said, "You're a Croatian mercenary; Tudjman is paying you to fight us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Osojnik, under interrogation -- or before we come to the interrogation, what did you see of Osojnik when you got there? What was the position of the houses and so on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: From the point they brought me to where the tent was, it was dusk already, but from what I could see, three or four houses were aflame, were burning. And from what I learnt from the other detainees, prisoners who were in the camp with me, I learnt that all the houses in the village were burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tent to which you were taken, what did the soldiers do to you when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: When they brought me to the tent, there was an officer inside. I don't know what rank, but he started to interrogate me. He asked about the forces, the positions of the Croatian so-called forces, and they started to beat me. The officer did as well, along with the soldiers. They beat me with all kinds of things, everything that they had at hand, to hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. At one point I did lose consciousness. I fainted. And when I came to, I later heard one of the officers, I think he had established connection with the command post, I think at Trebinje - I don't know for certain - but he asked them what he was to do with me. And he said, "What shall I do with him? He's got the same weapons as I have." And they said, "Bring him here," and that's how they came to take me to the camp Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken to Trebinje. In a vehicle, presumably. We can see it's about 20 kilometres, 30 kilometres. But did you stop on the way at any village or villages; and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes, we did stop in two places. They placed a bag over my head, a cotton bag, and we stopped at two places. I suppose they were hamlets or villages, and they said, "Here's an Ustasha." And then the members - rather, I don't know who they were, I heard the voices of children, civilians, and other people too in both these two places - I was beaten up very badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the villagers or by the soldiers who were guarding you, or were you not able to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure because I had this cotton bag over my head. From what I could hear, I heard the voices of children and women too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as being beaten, were you subjected to any other indignity on that occasion by the people in the street?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. They spat at me. That's the least of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the barracks at Trebinje, by whom were you received and then what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: At one place, I was taken over by three military policemen, and from there on they took me to the Trebinje barracks where I was put up, taken to a room with a large window and grills on the windows and a blackboard on the wall. I think it was a classroom of sorts. I spent some time there, I don't know how long exactly, and then the guard opened the door and several men came in, some with beards, some without, but all of them were wearing JNA uniforms. And one of them asked me whether I knew him, whether I recognised him, and I was taken aback and could barely see and said I didn't know who he was. But then when he smiled and I saw the tooth he had, the broken tooth he had, I remembered that he was one of the inhabitants of the city of Dubrovnik and that his name was Pero Miljevic. And then he said to me, "Well, we have got you now. It's your turn." And he told them that I was an Ustasha and that I had slaughtered around town, that I had set fire to Serb houses, that I had slaughtered Serbs, women and children. And then the other ten people that were there proceeded to beat me. This went on for some 15 or 20 minutes until an officer of the JNA came in and said, "That's enough. You've been beating him long enough."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in that room for a time until, in handcuffs, you were taken to another room where camouflage-uniformed soldiers, including more senior officers, were present?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you put in a chair, and if so, then what happened to your hands and feet?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Well, they started to interrogate me first. They asked about the positions of the Croatian army, the Croatian forces, and at that moment, I thought it best not to lie, to say -- to tell the truth, because there was nobody anywhere around. But they weren't satisfied with my answer. And one of them said, "You're going to spill the beans." And then they tied my hands to the chair and my legs to the legs of the chair. Then they turned the chair upside down, took the boots off my feet, and I don't know with what, a truncheon or something, they began to beat the soles of my feet. I know that I was in terrible pain, and I would have said anything I knew at that point, but I didn't know anything to confess to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember in any detail what you actually said to them about the Croatian forces of which you claim to be aware? What numbers did you put on the forces and so on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, when I could take the pain no longer, because it was excruciating, I said, "Right. I'll own up to everything. I'll recognise everything you say." And they put the chair upright again and I lied. I said that there were members of the Croatian National Guard Corps, the Zenga, I think I said five to six hundred. I said that there were artillery and tanks and mines all over the place. And they said to me, "Well, you could have owned up to that straight away and you wouldn't have received the beating you did."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken the next morning to Bileca barracks in an off-road vehicle, barely able to stand because of the beatings you had received?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on arrival there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, if you're moving on to another topic, might be a convenient moment. Mr. Hausvicka, we're going to adjourn now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hausvicka, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 to conclude your evidence. Would you remember not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include to members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
